title: The women in the garden
hook: the women are sent to charm him, and he stays unmoved (Buddhacarita 4)

segments.voice: Yesterday: death, the charioteer's last answer, and the world gone gray. Your line: the world goes gray.

The king has heard. His son came home from the road shaken, and now he won't stop thinking about old age and death. So the king reaches for the tool he trusts. He sends the prince to a beautiful garden outside the city, and sends the women of the court with him. Their task is plain: delight him, bring him back to the life of pleasure, make him forget what he saw. Music under the trees. Flowers. Laughter by the water. The poem lingers in this garden, and every line is built to pull a young man's attention away from one thought.
screen: `THE KING TRIES AGAIN.` → `A GARDEN, MUSIC, THE COURT'S WOMEN.` → `MAKE HIM FORGET.`

segments.voice: First, the women. They didn't choose this. They were sent, by a king, with a task. At first, the poem says, they hold back, shy before the prince. Then they're urged on, and they do what they were told: they sing and dance, tease and whisper, wander close in the flowering garden, described with all the color and play of court poetry. Second, the prince. He doesn't scold them or run. He simply isn't moved. He looks at the young women, bright and laughing, and sees what the road just taught him: this beauty will age, these bodies will sicken, these lives will end. He's not cold toward them. He's thinking about them more truly than the garden wants him to. Third, steadiness. Unmoved doesn't mean frozen, or proud, or disgusted. In the Anguttara Nikaya the Buddha names eight worldly conditions, gain and loss, good name and bad name, praise and blame, pleasure and pain, and describes a mind they don't overturn. In the garden only the pleasant half is pulling, and steadiness looks like quiet. And fourth, the cost to the king. Another remedy has failed, and the poem blames no one in the garden. The women did what they were asked. The prince did what he couldn't help. And before he goes home, a friend will try.
screen: `SENT, NOT CHOOSING.` · `HE SEES WHAT THE ROAD TAUGHT HIM.` · `UNMOVED IS NOT COLD.` · `THE KING'S REMEDY FAILS.` · then, large: `UNMOVED.`

segments.voice: Picture one thing that pulls at you on an ordinary day, the phone face-down on the table, a snack you're not hungry for, a show that starts the next episode on its own, and feel the pull honestly. Then breathe, and let it rise and pass without obeying it. You're not fighting it; you're just not moved.
steadiness. What the prince shows when the court women are sent to charm him in the garden: courteous, unmoved, already thinking of age and death beneath the beauty. Today's word.
Your line: unmoved. Courteous and kind, and still not carried off by the garden. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Buddhist teachers use the garden scene when speaking about sense pleasures and restraint, and in temple murals the prince is sometimes shown seated calmly among dancers and musicians.

fork.setup: you're the prince, in a flowering garden, surrounded by music and laughter meant to make you forget the road. what do you do?
options: give in and forget what you saw.
stay where you are, courteous, and keep seeing clearly.
shout at everyone and storm home.
fork.reveal: he stays unmoved. not cold, not angry: he sees the beauty and also where it ends.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prince who didn't like parties.
what it means: he isn't cold toward the women; what he saw on the road keeps him steady in the garden.
what a scholar hears: the canto is written with the lush detail of court poetry, so the reader feels the pull the prince is resisting.
recall: conscience, an inner sense of shame

chat.says: In the garden, was the prince just cold toward the women?
options: No, he stayed kind, but he saw their beauty would age and end.
Yes, he found pleasure disgusting and looked down on the women.
No, he enjoyed it, and only felt guilty about it much later.
chat.meaning: The poem has him unmoved but not cold: he sees beauty that will age and end, and thinks of them more truly.

Anguttara Nikaya.meaning: a collection of the Buddha's sayings sorted by number

eight worldly conditions.meaning: gain and loss, good and bad name, praise and blame, pleasure and pain

court poetry.meaning: ornate verse made for royal courts
